title: Can R&D advisors help with Section 174 capitalization?
description: R&D advisors help classify Section 174 expenditures, model Section 174A expensing versus amortization, and reconcile them with the Section 41 credit.
summary: R&D advisors can help U.S. businesses with Section 174 capitalization by classifying specified research or experimental expenditures, modeling Section 174A expensing versus 60-month or 10-year amortization elections, and reconciling those costs with Section 41 R&D tax credits, including Section 280C(c) elections and redesigned Form 6765 reporting. Domestic R&E is again immediately deductible for tax years beginning after 2024.

body.text: R&D advisors can help U.S. businesses with Section 174 capitalization by classifying specified research or experimental expenditures, modeling Section 174A expensing versus 60-month or 10-year amortization elections, and reconciling those costs with Section 41 R&D tax credits, including Section 280C(c) elections and redesigned Form 6765 reporting. Domestic R&E is again immediately deductible for tax years beginning after 2024.
Executive Overview: How Specialized R&D Advisors Support Section 174 Capitalization

Corporate accounting for research and development in the United States has undergone rapid legislative shifts between mandatory capitalization and immediate deduction, centering on Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 174 and the newly enacted Section 174A (IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-28). Specialized Research and Development (R&D) tax advisors play a direct, operational role in helping businesses manage Section 174 capitalization. Specifically, R&D advisors assist taxpayers across three core functions:

items: Regulatory Classification and Cost Tracing: Interpreting Internal Revenue Service (IRS) administrative guidance—most notably IRS Notice 2023-63 and its modifications in Notice 2024-12 and Rev. Proc. 2024-9—to identify specified research or experimental (SRE) expenditures, separate them from non-SRE business expenses, and trace direct and indirect costs across labor, supplies, software development, contract research, and long-term contracts under IRC Section 460 (IRS Notice 2023-63).

Multi-Year Financial Modeling and Transition Elections: Evaluating whether taxpayers should immediately expense domestic R&E costs under IRC Section 174A(a), elect optional amortization of at least 60 months under Section 174A(c), or elect 10-year amortization under IRC Section 59(e), while managing transition recoveries and retroactive small-business elections for 2022–2024 capitalized balances under IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-28 (KPMG Report on OBBBA Accounting Methods).

Reconciling Section 174 Capitalization with Section 41 R&D Tax Credits: Filtering the broad pool of Section 174/174A expenditures down to the narrower subset of Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) eligible for the IRC Section 41 tax credit, coordinating the IRC Section 280C(c) reduced-credit election, and preparing audit-ready documentation for the redesigned IRS Form 6765.

body.text: Statutory Evolution of Section 174 and Section 174A Capitalization Rules
Pre-TCJA Flexibility and Historical Enactment (Correction of 1954 vs. 1981 Origin)

Historically, Section 174 gave businesses flexibility in accounting for domestic research and experimental (R&E) expenditures: taxpayers could deduct R&E costs immediately in the year paid or incurred, defer and amortize them over a period of not less than 60 months, or charge them to a capital account (IRS Notice 2023-63).

items: Factual Correction on Statutory Origin: Primary IRS guidance in IRS Notice 2023-63 (Section 2.01(1)) confirms that former IRC Section 174 was first enacted in 1954 as part of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 (citing H.R. Rep. No. 1622, 83d Cong., 2d Sess. 33 (1954)) to resolve uncertainty over otherwise capitalizable R&E costs with no determinable useful life, rather than being introduced in 1981. Instead of creating Section 174, the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (Pub. L. No. 97-34) originally enacted the R&D tax credit (now codified under IRC Section 41) (DOJ Supreme Court Brief; Mercatus Center R&D Study).

body.text: The TCJA Mandatory Capitalization Era (Tax Years Beginning 2022–2024)

Under Section 13206(a) of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) of 2017 (Pub. L. 115-97, 131 Stat. 2054, enacted December 22, 2017), Congress eliminated the immediate deduction option under Section 174 for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021 (IRS Notice 2023-63; IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-28). Instead, taxpayers were required to capitalize all SRE expenditures and amortize them beginning at the midpoint of the taxable year in which the expenses were paid or incurred (IRS Notice 2023-63):

items: Domestic Research: 5-year (60-month) amortization period (IRS Notice 2023-63; RSM US Section 174 Overview).

Foreign Research: 15-year (180-month) amortization period for research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any U.S. territory or possession (IRS Notice 2023-63; RSM US Section 174 Overview).

body.text: This disparate recovery schedule penalized offshore research to incentivize domestic R&D placement, while mandatory capitalization compressed corporate cash flows and created unexpected taxable income and liquidity strain for pre-revenue startups and R&D-intensive technology and life sciences businesses.
IRS Notice 2023-63, Notice 2024-12, and Cost Categorization

To help businesses comply with TCJA Section 174 capitalization, R&D advisors apply the substantive rules introduced in IRS Notice 2023-63 (issued September 8, 2023) and subsequently clarified by Notice 2024-12 and Rev. Proc. 2024-9. Advisors use this guidance to classify and allocate expenditures across four complex operational areas:

items: Identification and Allocation of SRE Costs: Capturing direct and indirect wages (including benefits) of personnel who perform, supervise, or directly support R&E activities, materials and supplies consumed, and allocable facility and equipment overhead (such as rent, utilities, insurance, taxes, repairs, maintenance, and security used in R&E) (Plante Moran Section 174 Analysis; RSM US Section 174 Overview).

Software Development Activities: Under Section 5 of IRS Notice 2023-63, software development includes planning, designing, coding, and upgrades/enhancements that add functionality or materially increase speed or efficiency, whereas routine installation, configuration of purchased software, and employee training are excluded (Plante Moran Section 174 Analysis).

Research Performed Under Contract: Under Section 6 of IRS Notice 2023-63 (as modified by Notice 2024-12), advisors evaluate which party bears financial risk and which party retains rights to use or exploit the resulting SRE product (pilot model, process, formula, invention, technique, patent, or computer software) to determine whether the research recipient or the research provider must capitalize the contract costs (RSM US Section 174 Overview).

Long-Term Contracts under IRC Section 460: Assessing how SRE amortization allocable to long-term contracts interacts with the percentage-of-completion method (PCM) under Section 460 (RSM US Section 174 Overview; Grant Thornton Section 174 Alert).

body.text: Enactment of the OBBBA (2025), IRC Section 174A, and Transition Rules

On July 4, 2025, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), Public Law 119-21 (139 Stat. 72), was signed into law (IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-28; WilmerHale OBBBA Alert). Section 70302 of the OBBBA added IRC Section 174A, fundamentally changing the capitalization rules (IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-28; Surgent CPE OBBBA Analysis):

items: Permanent Immediate Expensing for Domestic R&E (Section 174A(a)): For amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, taxpayers may permanently and immediately deduct domestic R&E expenditures (including software development costs under Section 174A(d)(3)) (Surgent CPE OBBBA Analysis).

Continued 15-Year Amortization for Foreign R&E: The OBBBA retained the mandatory 15-year (180-month) capitalization and amortization requirement for foreign research expenditures under Section 174 (WilmerHale OBBBA Alert; Surgent CPE OBBBA Analysis).

Retroactive Relief for Eligible Small Businesses (OBBBA § 70302(f)(1)): Taxpayers that are not tax shelters and meet the IRC Section 448(c) gross receipts test—defined as having $31 million or less in average annual gross receipts over the prior three taxable years for their first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024—were permitted to elect to apply Section 174A retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, via amended returns or Administrative Adjustment Requests (AARs) (IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-28; ReedCorp Section 174A Guide).

Currency and Statutory Precision Update: Under IRC Section 448(c) and IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-28, the small-business threshold includes businesses that do not exceed $31 million ($31 million or less, rather than strictly "less than $31 million"), and the IRS established the hard filing deadline as the earlier of the statute of limitations for refund or July 6, 2026 (accounting for the weekend following July 4, 2026) (Baker Newman Noyes Rev. Proc. 2025-28 Alert; Tax Strategy Playbook Section 280C). Because the current date is November 11, 2026, that retroactive small-business filing window has closed (Surgent CPE OBBBA Analysis).

Unamortized 2022–2024 Balances for All Other Taxpayers (OBBBA § 70302(f)(2)): Under OBBBA Section 70302(f)(2) and IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-28, taxpayers with remaining unamortized domestic SRE balances from taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, may elect via automatic accounting method change procedures to deduct the remaining unamortized amount either in full in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, or ratably over the two taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024 (IRS Instructions for Form 6765).

body.text: Strategic Tax Planning and Elective Capitalization (Sections 174A(c) and 59(e))
Even with immediate domestic expensing restored under Section 174A(a), R&D advisors evaluate whether immediate deduction or elective capitalization produces the optimal multi-year tax outcome:

items: Section 174A(c) Election: Under IRC Section 174A(c) and Section 6.02 of IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-28, a taxpayer may elect to charge domestic R&E expenditures to a capital account and amortize them over a period of not less than 60 months. Once made, this election is binding for that taxable year and all subsequent years unless the taxpayer obtains IRS consent to change its method of accounting (Baker Newman Noyes Rev. Proc. 2025-28 Alert).
Section 59(e) Election: Alternatively, taxpayers may elect under IRC Section 59(e) to amortize qualified research expenditures ratably over a 10-year period (KPMG Report on OBBBA Accounting Methods).

Advisory Modeling Considerations (Analysis): Advisors model these elections against a company's profitability profile, Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) exposure, and expiring tax credits. For example, a technology or life sciences company operating at a tax loss may elect to capitalize and amortize R&E costs rather than increase a Net Operating Loss (NOL) carryforward, whereas a profitable enterprise generally defaults to immediate expensing under Section 174A(a) to reduce current-year tax liability.

body.text: Reconciling Section 174/174A Capitalization with Section 41 R&D Tax Credits
Structural Disparity in Statutory Scope

A primary reason companies engage R&D advisors for Section 174 capitalization is its direct statutory link to the IRC Section 41 Credit for Increasing Research Activities. While Section 174/174A governs whether research costs are deducted or capitalized, Section 41 provides a dollar-for-dollar reduction in tax liability (Mercatus Center R&D Study).

cells: Governs accounting treatment (immediate deduction vs. capitalization and amortization)

Direct and indirect R&E labor and benefits, consumed materials/supplies, contract research, allocable facility/equipment overhead (rent, utilities, depreciation), and patent procurement costs (IRS Notice 2023-63; Plante Moran Section 174 Analysis)
Provides a dollar-for-dollar general business tax credit

W-2 wages for qualified services, supplies consumed in research, rental/lease costs of computers, and applicable percentages of contract research (overhead and patent procurement excluded) (IRS Instructions for Form 6765; GBQ Form 6765 Updates)

body.text: To qualify as a QRE under IRC Section 41, an expenditure must first satisfy the gating requirement of being eligible under Section 174 (per IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A)), alongside the remaining prongs of the Section 41 Four-Part Test (IRS Notice 2023-63; The Tax Adviser QRA Documentation):

items: Section 174 Test / Permitted Purpose (Business Component Test): The expenditure must qualify as research or experimental under Section 174 and be undertaken to develop a new or improved business component (defined as a product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used in the taxpayer's trade or business) aimed at new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality (The Tax Adviser QRA Documentation).

Technological in Nature: The activity must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science (26 CFR 1.41-4; The Tax Adviser QRA Documentation).

Elimination of Uncertainty: The activity must be intended to discover information that eliminates technical uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design of the business component (The Tax Adviser QRA Documentation).

Process of Experimentation: Substantially all (at least 80%) of the research activities must constitute elements of a systematic process of experimentation—such as modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error—to evaluate one or more alternatives (The Tax Adviser QRA Documentation).

body.text: Because Section 174 is broader than Section 41, items such as patent procurement costs or indirect facility overhead fall within Section 174 R&E costs but are excluded from Section 41 QREs (IRS LB&I ASC 730 Directive).
Hypothetical Worked Example: Software Development Divergence and Internal Use Software (IUS)
To illustrate how advisors separate Section 174 capitalizable costs from Section 41 QREs, consider the following hypothetical scenario:

items: Scenario Assumptions (Hypothetical): A U.S. manufacturing corporation develops proprietary supply-chain optimization software and incurs $5,000,000 in total domestic software development expenditures during Year 1 (comprising developer wages, cloud computing costs, and external contractor fees).

Section 174 Capitalization Calculation (Hypothetical): Under mandatory TCJA Section 174 rules (2022–2024) or an affirmative 60-month amortization election under Section 174A(c), the entire $5,000,000 constitutes domestic software development expenditures (IRS Notice 2023-63; Surgent CPE OBBBA Analysis). Applying the statutory midpoint convention over a 5-year (60-month) recovery period:
Year 1 Amortization (6 months / 60 months = 10%): $5,000,000 multiplied by 0.10 equals $500,000.
Years 2 through 5 Amortization (12 months / 60 months = 20% per year): $5,000,000 multiplied by 0.20 equals $1,000,000 per year (totaling $4,000,000 across Years 2–5).
Year 6 Amortization (remaining 6 months / 60 months = 10%): $5,000,000 multiplied by 0.10 equals $500,000.
Total Recovered Over 6 Tax Years: $500,000 plus $4,000,000 plus $500,000 equals $5,000,000.

Section 41 QRE Filtration (Hypothetical): Upon technical review by an R&D advisor, only $3,000,000 of the expenditure relates to designing novel optimization algorithms through systematic trial-and-error that satisfies the Section 41 Four-Part Test. The remaining $2,000,000 ($5,000,000 minus $3,000,000 equals $2,000,000) is attributable to routine coding, basic maintenance, and standard user interface design, which must be accounted for under Section 174/174A but is excluded from the Section 41 credit base.

Internal Use Software (IUS) High Threshold of Innovation Test: Furthermore, if the software is developed primarily for the taxpayer's internal use (rather than for sale, lease, or license, or to interact with third parties outside general and administrative functions), IRS Instructions for Form 6765 confirm that it must also pass the three-part High Threshold of Innovation test in addition to the Four-Part Test:
The software is innovative, resulting in a substantial and economically significant reduction in cost or improvement in speed or other measurable objective criteria;

The development involves significant economic risk, where the taxpayer commits substantial resources and technical risk creates substantial uncertainty that those resources will be recovered within a reasonable period; and
The software is not commercially available for use by the taxpayer without modifications that themselves satisfy the first two requirements (IRS Instructions for Form 6765).

body.text: Navigating the IRC Section 280C(c) Intersection Across Tax Eras

To prevent taxpayers from claiming both a full deduction (or capital account basis) and a full research credit on the exact same dollar of expenditure, IRC Section 280C(c) requires coordination between Section 174/174A and Section 41 (Tax Strategy Playbook Section 280C).

items: Statutory Mechanism and Factual Clarification of TCJA vs. OBBBA Rules: Under the current rule restored by OBBBA Section 70302 (effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024), Section 280C(c)(1) requires a taxpayer's domestic R&E deduction (or capitalizable amount) to be reduced by the full amount of the Section 41 research credit claimed, unless the taxpayer makes a timely, irrevocable election under Section 280C(c)(2) on an original return (Item A of Form 6765) to claim a reduced research credit—which reduces the credit by the maximum corporate tax rate of 21% under IRC Section 11(b), leaving 79% of the gross credit (Tax Strategy Playbook Section 280C; Onshore Form 6765 Guide).

Important Correction/Clarification on the TCJA Period (2022–2024): The two distinct rules governing Section 280C(c) deduction reduction versus capital account reduction belong to different statutory periods: during the TCJA mandatory capitalization window (2022–2024), the amended text of Section 280C(c)(1) reduced the capital account only if the Section 41 credit exceeded the current-year amortization deduction—meaning most taxpayers could claim the full gross credit without reducing their capitalized basis (Baker Newman Noyes Rev. Proc. 2025-28 Alert). When the OBBBA enacted Section 174A for 2025 onward (and retroactively for electing small businesses), it restored the strict dollar-for-dollar deduction/capital reduction rule, and IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-28 (Section 5.03) granted retroactive small-business electors until July 6, 2026, to make or revoke a late Section 280C(c)(2) election on amended 2022–2024 returns (Baker Newman Noyes Rev. Proc. 2025-28 Alert; Tax Strategy Playbook Section 280C).

cells: Forego Reduced Credit Election: Capital account reduced only if credit exceeded current-year amortization (or deduction loss spread over 60 months) (Baker Newman Noyes Rev. Proc. 2025-28 Alert)
Maximize current-year gross credit cash flow
Immediate Expensing under IRC Section 174A(a) (IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-28)

Make Reduced Credit Election (Sec. 280C(c)(2)): Accept 21% credit reduction (keeping 79% of credit) to avoid dollar-for-dollar reduction of 100% immediate deduction (Tax Strategy Playbook Section 280C)
Preserve 100% immediate R&E deduction in current tax year

body.text: Specialized Advisory Methodology
Redesigned IRS Form 6765 Reporting Requirements

The need for specialized R&D advisors has intensified due to the IRS's overhaul of Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) (IRS Instructions for Form 6765). As confirmed by the finalized IRS Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) and practitioner analyses (Massie Tax Credits Form 6765 Analysis; GBQ Form 6765 Updates):

items: Section E (Other Information — Mandatory for 2025 Returns): Requires every claimant to report the total number of business components generating QREs (Line 37), the amount of officer wages included in QREs (Line 38), whether the taxpayer acquired or disposed of a major portion of a trade or business during the tax year (Line 39), whether new categories of QREs were claimed, and whether the ASC 730 Directive was applied (Line 41) (Massie Tax Credits Form 6765 Analysis; GBQ Form 6765 Updates).

Section G (Business Component Information — Optional for Tax Years Beginning Before 2026; Mandatory Starting in Tax Year 2026 for Non-Exempt Filers): Requires project-level reporting by business component covering at least 80% of total QREs up to a maximum of 50 business components ("80%/Top 50"), including the business component type, software classification (internal use, non-internal use, or dual-function), the information sought to be discovered, and QRE breakdowns by component (IRS Instructions for Form 6765; Onshore Form 6765 Guide).

body.text: Proprietary AI Infrastructure (TaxTrex and creditARMOR) and the Six-Eye Review

items: TaxTrex AI Platform: A specialized Do-It-Yourself (DIY) B2B Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) AI language model trained on U.S. R&D tax credit rules. Operating at a $395 per month tier, TaxTrex captures wage data, automates technical surveys with time-stamping and tiered user access, and compresses the qualification and documentation generation phase to approximately 90 minutes.

creditARMOR Audit Management and Risk Platform: An R&D tax credit audit management and risk-treatment insurance platform that tracks ongoing research time and QREs while covering IRS audit defense expenses—including CPA, tax attorney, and specialist consultant fees.

Mandatory Six-Eye Review (Human-in-the-Loop Safeguard): Before any TaxTrex or advisory claim is finalized into Form 6765 and audit substantiation narratives, it undergoes a mandatory review by three distinct specialists:

Qualified Engineer: Verifies that the technical narrative accurately reflects mechanical, electrical, or software engineering principles and distinguishes qualifying prototypes from routine production tools.
Scientist: Validates that biological, chemical, or physical science claims adhere to the scientific method and provide iterative evidence of systematic experimentation meeting the 80% threshold.

CPA or Enrolled Agent: Verifies general ledger consistency (such as depreciation vs. Section 174 capitalization/expense), QRE calculations, and Section 280C(c) elections. If AI outputs contain inaccuracies or hallucinations, reviewers restart the AI workflow or prepare the claim manually.

body.text: Regional Innovation Case Studies and State-Level Tax Liquidity Mechanisms
R&D advisors also coordinate federal Section 174 capitalization and Section 41 credits with state-level innovation regimes:

items: Huntington, West Virginia ("IDEA District"): Along Fourth Avenue between Downtown Huntington and Marshall University, the Marshall IDEA District (Impossible Doesn't Exist Anymore) is a $200 million-plus innovation corridor linking academic biomedical and institutional research with private commercialization (WV Chamber of Commerce Huntington Spotlight; Fairmount Properties Marshall University). Advisors evaluate commercializing firms' biomedical and manufacturing activities against both the federal Four-Part Test and West Virginia tax incentives.

Lexington, Kentucky (Autonomous Marine Systems): Engineering specialists evaluate firms developing Unmanned Surface Vehicles (USVs) and Unmanned Underwater Vehicles (UUVs) that integrate marine perception sensors, radar processing, and acoustic telemetry to solve real-time sensor-fusion and obstacle-avoidance uncertainties in GPS-denied or high-turbidity water environments, separating Section 41 QREs from the broader Section 174 cost pool.

Kansas Transferable R&D Tax Credit (K.S.A. 79-32,182b): To help cash-constrained R&D firms offset the liquidity impact of Section 174 capitalization, Kansas law (K.S.A. 79-32,182b, for tax year 2023 and thereafter) allows taxpayers without current tax liability to transfer their full R&D credit one time to another person (documented via Form K-260) to claim against Kansas income tax liability (Kansas Department of Revenue Form K-53). Furthermore, the credit allowable in any single taxable year is limited to 25% of the total credit plus applicable carryforwards, with remaining unused credit carried forward in 25% annual increments until exhausted (Kansas Department of Revenue Form K-53).

North Dakota Alternative Simplified Computation (N.D.C.C. § 57-38-30.5): Under North Dakota Century Code § 57-38-30.5 (effective beginning tax year 2019), taxpayers conducting qualified in-state research (adopting IRC Section 41(d)) may elect the Alternative Simplified Computation (ASC) method—modeled on IRC Section 41(c)(5)—equal to 17.5% of the first $100,000 of North Dakota alternative excess R&D expenses plus 5.6% of excess expenses over $100,000 (North Dakota Office of State Tax Commissioner; FindLaw N.D.C.C. § 57-38-30.5).

body.text: IRS Audit Defense and the Taxpayer's Burden of Proof

In IRS examinations, the taxpayer bears the full burden of proof to substantiate both that expenditures were incurred under Section 174/174A and that activities satisfied all elements of IRC Section 41(d)(1) through contemporaneous documentation (IRS Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide (RCCATG); The Tax Adviser QRA Documentation).

items: Tier 1 Issue History and Audit Techniques Guides (ATGs): The IRS designated Research Credit Claims as a Tier I compliance issue from 2007 until the tiered issue system was retired in 2012, and examiners continue to apply specialized Audit Techniques Guides (ATGs) that reject unsupported, prepackaged estimates (Mercatus Center R&D Study; IRS Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide (RCCATG)).

LB&I ASC 730 Directives: For Large Business & International (LB&I) taxpayers that expense R&D on audited financial statements pursuant to ASC 730, the IRS issued its 2017 Directive (LB&I-04-0917-005, later updated by LB&I-04-0820-0016 in 2020), establishing a safe-harbor framework for determining adjusted ASC 730 financial statement R&D eligible for Section 41 while requiring specific subtractions for patent costs, prototype overhead, and foreign research (IRS LB&I ASC 730 Directive; The Tax Adviser IRS R&D Policing History).
